opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it was a genuine turning point, though perhaps not quite in the way it's often portrayed. What happened around 2012, with AlexNet winning the ImageNet competition by a huge margin, was that people suddenly realized that ideas that had been around for decades (multi-layer neural networks trained by backpropagation, convolutional architectures going back to Fukushima and LeCun) actually worked remarkably well once you had enough data and enough computation. The GPUs and the large labeled datasets were the missing ingredients.

So in one sense it wasn't a conceptual revolution. The underlying mathematics was well understood. But in practical terms it was enormous. For the first time we had systems that could do perceptual tasks, recognizing objects in images and later transcribing speech and translating between languages, at a level that was actually useful. And those were precisely the areas where classical AI had struggled. We had decent methods for reasoning and planning, but connecting them to raw perceptual input was always the bottleneck.

What I'd emphasize, though, is that it also changed the culture of the field, and not entirely for the better. There was a shift toward treating AI as an empirical exercise: you build a big circuit, you train it end to end, and you see what comes out. That's produced impressive results, but we often don't understand why these systems work, or when they're going to fail. With classical approaches, you knew what the system knew and how it reasoned. With a deep network you have billions of parameters and very limited insight into what's going on inside.

And I think that has real consequences for safety. If you don't understand how a system works, it's very hard to give guarantees about its behavior. The deep learning approach also tends to bake in the standard model of AI: you specify a fixed objective, a loss function, and optimize it as hard as you can. That's the very paradigm I've argued is fundamentally flawed, because we can't specify objectives completely and correctly.

So I'd say 2012 was the moment AI went from being a fairly niche academic field to a major economic and technological force. It accelerated everything enormously. But I don't think deep learning by itself is the whole answer to general-purpose intelligence. I suspect we'll need to combine its strengths with the expressive power of structured representations, things like first-order logic and probabilistic programming, to get systems that learn efficiently, reason reliably, and that we can actually understand and control.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's important to put it in context, because deep learning didn't come out of nowhere. The basic ideas—multilayer networks trained by gradient descent—had been around since the 1980s, and in some form since the 1960s. What changed around 2012 was really three things coming together: much larger datasets, like ImageNet; much more computation, particularly the use of GPUs; and a handful of engineering refinements that made it practical to train deeper networks. So the breakthrough was less a conceptual revolution and more a demonstration that these methods, at scale, could do things that the field had been struggling with for decades, particularly in computer vision and then speech recognition.

That demonstration mattered enormously, though. For most of the history of AI, we'd made progress by building systems out of components that we understood—logical reasoning, probabilistic models, search algorithms. Perception was the piece that was always embarrassing. We couldn't get machines to reliably recognise objects in images, and that was a serious obstacle to putting AI systems into the real world. Deep learning essentially solved perception, or at least made it good enough that it stopped being the bottleneck. And that in turn unlocked a huge amount of investment and attention, which is really what transformed the trajectory of the field.

But I'd also sound a note of caution about how we interpret it. There's a tendency to think that because deep learning works, we now understand intelligence, or that scaling up these systems will take us all the way to general-purpose AI. I don't think that's right. These systems are extraordinarily good at learning mappings from inputs to outputs when you have enough data, but they don't obviously give us the capacity for reasoning, for building and using explicit knowledge, for planning over long horizons—things that are central to intelligence as we understand it. In some ways, the success of deep learning has caused us to forget a lot of what we'd learned in the previous sixty years.

So I'd say its significance is twofold. It removed a major practical barrier and brought AI into the real economy and into public consciousness in a way nothing had before. And it also raised the stakes, because once systems become capable enough to matter, the question of whether we've built them correctly—whether they'll actually do what we want—stops being academic and becomes urgent.

astra-6.text:
I think it was a very significant breakthrough, although it’s useful to distinguish the breakthrough in performance from the invention of the underlying ideas. Neural networks had been around for decades, and many of the techniques used to train them were already familiar. What changed was that we had much more data, much more computation, and ways of putting those together that made the systems work substantially better.

The most visible example was image recognition. Instead of researchers painstakingly designing features that might help a computer recognize an object, you could train a network to learn useful features from examples. And the improvement was large enough that it changed the direction of research very quickly. Similar advances in speech recognition helped make clear that this wasn’t confined to one problem.

But I wouldn’t equate that with solving artificial intelligence. Recognizing an object in an image is an important capability; it isn’t the same as understanding how the world works, reasoning about what might happen, or deciding what to do. So I see 2012 as a major advance in our ability to learn from data, and an enormous catalyst for investment and practical applications, rather than a point at which all the other problems in AI suddenly disappeared.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it was a very important breakthrough, although we should be clear about what changed. Neural networks had been around for decades. What came together was enough computing power, enough data, and techniques that allowed us to train much larger networks effectively. Around 2012, particularly in image recognition, that combination produced a dramatic improvement over the existing methods.

That changed the field’s sense of what was possible. Tasks like recognizing objects or understanding speech, which had resisted progress for a long time, suddenly became much more tractable. It also attracted enormous investment, which accelerated the process further.

But I wouldn’t equate that with having solved intelligence. Learning to map an input to an output is an important capability, but it doesn’t by itself give you the whole range of abilities we associate with intelligence—reasoning, planning, understanding how the world works. So I see it as a major advance in the tools available to AI, rather than a complete account of how to build an intelligent system.
